title: Put a dropped chain back on a child's bike: lay it on the chainring and turn the crank
instruction: The chain has come off. Put it back on.
context: A dropped chain is the most common roadside bike fault, and children's bikes drop them often. The fix is quick but dexterous: lay a few links onto the chainring's teeth and turn the crank so the ring draws the rest on. Done right, the crank then turns freely with the chain staying on.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table. A real child's 16-inch single-speed drivetrain is clamped in a bench stand (black steel, fixed to the table) with the bike's length running left-right and its drive side facing the arms: bottom-bracket axle at (36, 17), 13 cm above the table, in a blue steel frame shell (3.9 cm across, inboard); a 28-tooth steel chainring (pitch circle 11.3 cm across) with a 95 mm black aluminium crank arm and a 7 x 6.5 x 2.2 cm resin pedal, the crank pointing down and 30 degrees toward the left; a 16-tooth steel rear sprocket on a freewheeling hub 30 cm to the right (y = -13), same height; a 1/2 x 1/8 inch steel chain of 70 links (about 350 g). The chain has come off the chainring to the inside: it is still meshed on the rear sprocket and hangs slack round the frame's bottom-bracket shell, 8 mm inboard of the chainring. Nothing else is on the table. Both arms start at the ready pose with open grippers.
scoring: Judged from the video and, at the end, a photo and one hand test. On the chainring: at least 10 consecutive rollers sit between the chainring's teeth (about 130 degrees of wrap). Proven: while the chain stayed on the chainring, the crank turned at least one full revolution (either direction), and the chain is still for 1 s at the end. 1.0: on the chainring and proven. 0.5: on the chainring at the end but the crank never turned a full revolution with it on (for example the chain is only balanced on the teeth). 0.25: 4 to 9 rollers between the chainring's teeth at the end. 0: anything else, including the chain knocked off the rear sprocket, or nothing done. If the chain falls off the chainring during the turn, the count starts again.
reset_notes: Lift the chain off the chainring to the inside and let it hang on the bottom-bracket shell, still on the rear sprocket; turn the crank to 30 degrees from straight down.
fidelity: Isaac Lab-Arena YAM station. Chainring, crank, pedal and sprocket are an articulation with free bearings; the chain is 70 rigid links (roller and side plates) on hinges with 4 degrees of side flex, its loop closed by a joint outside the articulation. Teeth are boxes, not true tooth profiles; there is no chain lubrication or wear. The rear hub freewheels both ways.
